title: AI’s Impact on Labor and Hiring - Liberty Street Economics
gist: New York Fed research director Kartik B. Athreya (the raw record's author field reads 'peterstevens', a CMS handle; the text is bylined Athreya) argues AI's labor-market footprint so far is a skill-mix and hiring-composition shift, not a layoff wave: regional survey AI adoption jumped from 25% to 40% of service firms and 16% to 26% of manufacturers between 2024 and 2025, yet firms report very few AI-driven layoffs and overwhelmingly plan to retrain rather than fire. His non-consensus warning is that the most profound long-run effect may be on the demand side — AI-supercharged social media tilting consumption toward zero-sum positional goods — rather than on the supply side of labor.

themes.theme: Household AI Anxiety vs. Observed Firm Behavior

insights.claim: New York Fed research from October 2024 found that individuals who had been exposed to generative AI tools ended up with bleaker expectations for job availability and income inequality, meaning direct AI exposure worsens rather than reassures worker sentiment.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Consumer-expectations surveys will keep showing AI-driven pessimism even while hard labor data stays benign — fade sentiment-driven recession calls sourced from AI anxiety.
insights.quote: individuals who had been exposed to generative AI tools appeared to be left with bleaker expectations for job availability and income inequality.

insights.claim: A September 2025 New York Fed regional survey found AI adoption rising quickly across industries while firms reported very few AI-driven layoffs, contradicting the popular narrative that AI is already destroying jobs at scale.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Positioning for an imminent AI unemployment shock is early; watch initial claims and job-postings composition rather than layoff headlines.
insights.quote: while AI adoption is rising quickly across industries, firms report very few AI-driven layoffs

insights.claim: Firms in the New York Fed's regional survey anticipate more reductions in hiring plans going forward, especially for college-educated workers, so the AI adjustment shows up as a hiring freeze concentrated in white-collar entry points rather than as terminations.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Expect degraded new-grad and white-collar hiring rates; a screen on staffing firms, education/credentialing and graduate-heavy employers is warranted.
insights.quote: firms do anticipate more reductions in hiring plans going forward—especially for college-educated workers

themes.theme: Adoption Curve in the Regional Survey Data

insights.claim: New York Fed Regional Business Survey data show the share of service firms using AI rose from 25 percent in 2024 to 40 percent in 2025 with 44 percent expected within the next six months, while manufacturers went from 16 to 26 percent and expect 33 percent.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Service-sector AI penetration is ~14 points ahead of manufacturing and flattening (40 to 44 in six months), suggesting enterprise software seat growth in services decelerates while industrial AI still has runway.
insights.locator: Rapid Adoption of AI Across Industries

insights.claim: Recruiting patterns are bifurcating under AI: some firms are cutting hiring because AI automates tasks while others are increasing hiring for AI-proficient workers, so aggregate employment data understate the churn happening beneath the surface.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Net payroll prints will look uneventful while the AI-skill wage premium widens — trade the dispersion, not the aggregate.
insights.quote: some firms are reducing hiring because AI automates tasks, while others are increasing hiring for AI-proficient workers

themes.theme: Jobs as Task Bundles and Retraining Over Firing

insights.claim: The New York Fed's read of the evidence is that AI's labor-market impact so far has more to do with changing skill requirements than with eliminating jobs, an explicitly time-qualified conclusion rather than a permanent one.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: This is the Fed's working assumption for the employment side of its dual mandate — it implies no AI-driven easing bias until layoff data actually turn.
insights.quote: AI’s labor-market impact has more to do with changing skill requirements than eliminating jobs—at least so far

insights.claim: Treating each job as a 'bundle of tasks' rather than a single function is the right analytical frame for AI displacement, because when AI takes over some tasks it frees teams to work on other areas of production and respond to changing demand.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Screen companies by task exposure, not occupation labels — firms whose headcount sits on task bundles with high residual value are mispriced as 'AI roadkill'.
insights.quote: it’s useful to think about each job as encompassing a “bundle of tasks” rather than a single function

insights.claim: Work by Luis Garicano and coauthors implies that safety from AI is not limited to physical and personal-care work, undercutting the common assumption that only manual and caregiving jobs survive automation.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: The 'buy trades and healthcare aides, sell knowledge work' AI trade is too simplistic per Fed research staff.
insights.quote: we need not assume, as some have speculated, that AI adoption will only spare jobs that focus on physical tasks and personal care.

insights.claim: When directly surveyed about AI plans, firms overwhelmingly said they intend to retrain workers rather than fire them, and Survey of Consumer Expectations data show workers also place significant value on AI training.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Both employer and employee demand point at corporate reskilling and AI-training platforms as a funded budget line, not a discretionary one.
insights.quote: firms overwhelmingly intend to retrain workers rather than fire them as they adopt AI
insights.locator: Businesses Expect Growth in Share of Workers Retraining for AI Use

insights.claim: The New York Fed frames AI's short-run effect as evolutionary rather than disruptive and anchors it to historical technology diffusion lags, citing the long gap between the invention of steam power and its replacement by modern propulsion on American rivers.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: The Fed's base case is slow absorption — which argues against AI-driven productivity showing up in near-term potential-GDP or r-star estimates.
insights.quote: A classic example is that of the long duration between the invention of steam power and its replacement with modern propulsion on American rivers.

themes.theme: Specialization as the Real Tail Risk

insights.claim: The genuine economic danger from AI is not automation itself but specialization: because each worker supplies only a narrow set of tasks, a sudden collapse in the value of that one skill is catastrophic in a way it would not be for a self-sufficient producer.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Reframes AI risk as an uninsured idiosyncratic skill shock — the investable corollary is demand for income insurance, retraining and safety-net products.
insights.quote: the real friction is that our specialization leaves us vulnerable to a sudden collapse in the value of the only skills we may have.
insights.locator: Street Level Observations: AI Risks to Watch

insights.claim: A senior Fed research director flags retraining, a thicker safety net and universal basic income as the policy responses under public debate while warning each could carry poorly understood unintended consequences, signaling the labor market will remain a live research and policy focus at the New York Fed.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Expect fiscal-transfer proposals tied to AI to gain airtime — a duration-negative, deficit-positive medium-term risk.
insights.quote: The public debate recognizes this in its focus on retraining, a thicker safety net, universal basic income (UBI), and so on. Each of these responses could carry unintended consequences

insights.claim: AI will likely make many goods and services far cheaper, effectively raising real incomes, which means the disinflationary and real-wealth channel of AI matters as much as the employment channel.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Supports a structurally disinflationary goods-and-services impulse — relevant to long-end real yields and to pricing power assumptions in services businesses.
insights.quote: AI will likely render many goods and services far cheaper than at present, making us effectively richer.

insights.claim: As AI-enabled algorithms supercharge social media platforms, consumer spending could tilt toward goods whose value is relative rather than absolute — the status-driven products influencers promote — shifting the composition of consumption away from need-based categories.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for positional/status categories (luxury, experiences, creator-economy commerce) and for ad-driven platforms that monetize comparison.
insights.quote: our spending habits could tilt toward things whose value is more relative in nature
insights.locator: Second, it’s also crucial to account for

insights.claim: A consumption economy built on status comparison is wasteful and zero-sum in the economist's sense because only a few experiences can be 'best', and the New York Fed's research director speculates this demand-side effect may prove more profound in the long run than AI's smoothly absorbed supply-side effects.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: A rare official-sector welfare critique of the attention-economy business model — a leading indicator of regulatory interest in AI-amplified social platforms.
insights.quote: Constantly chasing those outcomes would also be a zero-sum game, since there can only be a few “best” meal experiences
insights.locator: A world in which our consumption patterns

insights.claim: The New York Fed's summary judgment is that evidence on AI adoption suggests more muted effects on labor and hiring so far, even though anxiety about AI remains undiminished — an explicit gap between measured impact and perceived impact.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: The measured-vs-perceived gap is the tradable inefficiency: sentiment-sensitive assets can overreact to AI job-loss narratives the Fed's own data do not yet support.
insights.quote: the evidence on adoption suggests more muted effects on labor and hiring so far, but anxiety remains just the same.
